question: A student must choose a program of four courses from a menu of courses consisting of English, Algebra, Geometry, History, Art, and Latin. This program must contain English and at least one mathematics course. In how many ways can this program be chosen?
solution:
Because English must be included, a four-course program can be chosen by deciding which two of the other five courses to omit. Each omitted pair determines exactly one program, and every program containing English has exactly one omitted pair.

There are \(5\cdot4\) ways to select a first and second omitted course. Each unordered pair is counted twice, once in each order, so the number of pairs is
\[
\frac{5\cdot4}{2}=10.
\]
Algebra and Geometry are the only mathematics courses. A program contains no mathematics exactly when those two courses are the omitted pair. Removing this one forbidden pair leaves
\[
10-1=\boxed{9}
\]
programs, choice C.

solutionMethods.explanation:
Include English first, leaving three courses to choose. A valid program contains either exactly one mathematics course or both mathematics courses.

With exactly one mathematics course, there are \(2\) choices between Algebra and Geometry. We then choose two of History, Art, and Latin. There are \(3\) ways to do that, determined by which one of those three courses is left out. This gives \(2\cdot3=6\) programs.

With both Algebra and Geometry, the final course can be any one of History, Art, and Latin, giving \(3\) programs.

These cases include every valid program and do not overlap because their numbers of mathematics courses differ. The total is
\[
6+3=\boxed{9},
\]
choice C.

reference.question: A student must choose a program of four courses from a menu of courses consisting of English, Algebra, Geometry, History, Art, and Latin. This program must contain English and at least one mathematics course. In how many ways can this program be chosen?
reference.solution:
Method 1: Choose the two courses to omit

Because English must be included, a four-course program can be chosen by deciding which two of the other five courses to omit. Each omitted pair determines exactly one program, and every program containing English has exactly one omitted pair.

There are \(5\cdot4\) ways to select a first and second omitted course. Each unordered pair is counted twice, once in each order, so the number of pairs is
\[
\frac{5\cdot4}{2}=10.
\]
Algebra and Geometry are the only mathematics courses. A program contains no mathematics exactly when those two courses are the omitted pair. Removing this one forbidden pair leaves
\[
10-1=\boxed{9}
\]
programs, choice C.

Method 2: Count programs with one or two mathematics courses

Include English first, leaving three courses to choose. A valid program contains either exactly one mathematics course or both mathematics courses.

With exactly one mathematics course, there are \(2\) choices between Algebra and Geometry. We then choose two of History, Art, and Latin. There are \(3\) ways to do that, determined by which one of those three courses is left out. This gives \(2\cdot3=6\) programs.

With both Algebra and Geometry, the final course can be any one of History, Art, and Latin, giving \(3\) programs.

These cases include every valid program and do not overlap because their numbers of mathematics courses differ. The total is
\[
6+3=\boxed{9},
\]
choice C.

edges.reason: A complement can be defined and listed directly as the elements of U not in A, and counted as |U| minus |A|. The fact that A together with its complement makes U is a helpful framing.
Contrasting disjoint alternatives with sequential choices helps choose an operation. An array of shirts and trousers establishes the product principle independently of the addition rule.
The combined counting criterion contains multiplicative stages within classified cases; the stage-wise multiplication principle is directly used in those parts.
The criterion distinguishes combinations from permutations, requiring the ordered-selection concept for that contrast even though unordered selection can be introduced independently.
The application criterion computes unordered counts by categories, containing combination-number evaluation within those categories.
